title: The Second Rule: Push and Acceleration

t: Push a trolley twice as hard. Does it speed up twice as fast?
Push a trolley, then push it twice as hard. Does it accelerate twice as much?
Double the force on a trolley. Is the acceleration doubled?
If the net force on a body doubles, what happens to its acceleration?
sub: There is a rule. The rule is exact, and it is one of the most useful things ever discovered.
Newton found the rule, and it works for everything from marbles to rockets.
Newton's second law: F = ma. The relationship is linear in both force and mass.
Newton's second law: F_net = ma. The acceleration is directly proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.

question: Same push, but the trolley is twice as heavy. How much acceleration now?
Same push, double the mass. What happens to the acceleration?
A force F produces acceleration a on mass m. What acceleration does F produce on 2m?
If F = ma, what is a when m is doubled and F is held constant?
note: Heavier things are harder to get moving. Guess how much harder.
Predict before checking. The relationship is exact, not a guess.
Form a hypothesis from F = ma before testing.
Apply a = F/m: doubling m halves a. Predict, then verify.

t: Keep the push the same. Change the mass. Watch how the acceleration changes.
Set the push to 4. Try mass 1, then mass 2, then mass 3. Watch the net force arrow — it stays the same, but the trolley accelerates less with more mass.
goal: Reach the goal speed. Try different masses — heavier means slower to get going.
Reach the target v. Confirm a = F/m by varying mass at constant F.

t: Find the push that reaches the goal with mass 2. Then set mass to 4 — what push do you need now? Work it out before you test.
Determine the force needed to reach the goal at m=2. Then predict the force needed at m=4 (same target v) before testing. Verify a = F/m quantitatively.
goal: Reach the goal. The push you need scales with the mass — that is F = ma.
Reach the target v. Confirm F ∝ m for fixed a, verifying the second law.

t: Push equals mass times how fast it speeds up. That is the rule.
Force = mass × acceleration. That is Newton's second law.
Newton's second law: F = ma. Force equals mass times acceleration. The units are newtons (N), where 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s².
Newton's second law: F_net = ma. The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration. A vector equation; valid in inertial frames.
sub: More push, more acceleration. More mass, less acceleration. The rule is exact.
Double the push, double the acceleration. Double the mass, halve the acceleration. F = ma.
F = ma is a vector equation. The acceleration points in the direction of the net force. 1 N accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s².
F_net = ma is the foundational equation of mechanics. It holds in all inertial frames and breaks down only at relativistic speeds or quantum scales.

t: A rocket is just F = ma with a very big push and a very small mass.
Rockets work because F = ma: big force, small mass, huge acceleration.
A Saturn V produces 35 million newtons to accelerate 3 million kg. That is F = ma at the scale of a building.
The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation derives from F = ma: Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m_f). Every gram of dry mass costs delta-v.

q: You push a 2 kg trolley with 6 newtons of force. What is its acceleration?
A 2 kg trolley is pushed with 6 N. What is its acceleration?
F = 6 N, m = 2 kg. Find a.
Given F_net = 6 N and m = 2 kg, compute a.
why: F = ma means a = F ÷ m. So 6 ÷ 2 = 3. The trolley accelerates at 3 metres per second per second.
a = F/m = 6/2 = 3 m/s². The force is split across the mass: each kilogram gets 3 newtons.
Rearranging F = ma: a = F/m = 6 N / 2 kg = 3 m/s². Each second, the speed increases by 3 m/s.
a = F_net/m = 6/2 = 3 m/s². By the second law, the acceleration vector is parallel to F_net with magnitude F/m.

q: Same push, but the mass doubles. What happens to the acceleration?
Double the mass, keep the force the same. What happens to a?
If m → 2m at constant F, what happens to a?
At constant F_net, if m doubles, how does a change?
why: a = F ÷ m. If m gets twice as big, the answer is half as much. Heavier things accelerate less with the same push.
a = F/m. Doubling m doubles the denominator, so a halves. Inverse proportionality.
a = F/m. With F constant, a ∝ 1/m. Doubling m halves a.
a = F_net/m is inverse in m. At fixed F, a(2m) = a(m)/2. The relationship is hyperbolic.
